messages.content: I want to develop continual visual recognition that can distinguish genuinely novel classes from recurring appearance shifts, without task boundaries or stored images. The target is novelty-detection AUROC ≥0.90 when unseen classes and recurring appearance shifts coexist, while limiting the mean old-class accuracy decline from post-acquisition performance to ≤5 percentage points.

Those are two linked requirements: recognize when a class is genuinely unseen, even while familiar appearances change and recur, and retain recognition of previously acquired classes. The setting does not provide task boundaries or permit stored images. The AUROC target applies when unseen classes and recurring appearance shifts coexist; the accuracy constraint is a mean decline relative to post-acquisition performance.
What is the distinction the system needs to make when appearances change?

An appearance shift changes how something looks; it does not, by itself, make its class novel. A novel class is one the system has not previously acquired. The challenge is not to treat a returning change in appearance as evidence of a new class merely because it looks different, while still detecting genuinely unseen classes.
Does “recurring” matter, rather than just saying that appearances can shift?

Yes. The goal explicitly includes appearance shifts that recur, so the distinction is not limited to a single, one-off change. A shifted appearance may be encountered again, and the recognition objective remains to separate that kind of variation from genuine class novelty.
And what does the absence of task boundaries mean here?

It means the continual-recognition setting cannot rely on supplied boundaries that divide the experience into distinct tasks. Such a boundary would not be available to announce when to reconsider what is familiar or novel. That condition does not, on its own, specify the sequence of observations or how the system must be implemented.
Should I read “without stored images” as forbidding every possible form of memory?

No. The stated constraint is that images are not stored. It does not specify a complete rule for every other possible form of retained information, so it would be too strong to restate it as a ban on all memory. Nor does it prescribe a particular alternative to image storage.
I want the novelty result to hold in the difficult case, not only when new classes appear by themselves.

That matches the condition on the target: novelty-detection AUROC must be at least 0.90 when unseen classes and recurring appearance shifts coexist. The requirement is not merely to detect novelty in isolation from shifts; the distinction matters precisely when both are present.
What does AUROC tell me in this wording?

AUROC is the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. Here it expresses novelty-detection performance across possible decision thresholds. The required value is ≥0.90; the goal does not specify one operating threshold or claim that every individual novelty decision must be correct.
Does the 0.90 requirement say that every unseen class and every returning shift must individually reach that value?

No such per-class or per-shift requirement is stated. The specified target is novelty-detection AUROC ≥0.90 under coexistence of unseen classes and recurring appearance shifts. How results would be broken down further is not given.
How should I understand the accuracy constraint alongside that detection target?

Novelty detection is not the only objective. Recognition of old classes also needs to be retained: the mean decline in old-class accuracy, measured against post-acquisition performance, must be no more than 5 percentage points. A strong novelty-detection AUROC would not by itself establish that the old-class accuracy constraint is satisfied.
Why specify percentage points instead of a percentage decline?

Percentage points describe an absolute difference between accuracy percentages. For a purely hypothetical illustration, going from 90% accuracy to 85% accuracy is a decline of 5 percentage points. That arithmetic illustrates the unit; it is not a reported performance value for this goal.
Is the comparison against performance before a class was acquired?

No. The stated reference is post-acquisition performance. The retention requirement compares old-class accuracy with that reference, rather than with performance from before acquisition. No particular measurement schedule is specified.
Does a mean decline of at most 5 percentage points guarantee that no individual old class loses more than that?

Not necessarily. “Mean” makes this an average constraint on old-class accuracy decline, not an explicit maximum for each individual class. The requirement should remain stated as a mean decline of ≤5 percentage points from post-acquisition performance.
So neither target should be treated as a substitute for the other?

Right. Novelty-detection AUROC ≥0.90 addresses distinguishing unseen classes amid recurring appearance shifts. Mean old-class accuracy decline ≤5 percentage points addresses retaining performance after acquisition. The goal calls for both, under the stated no-task-boundary and no-stored-image constraints.
Would a returning shifted appearance count as novel simply because the system encounters it at a different time?

Not on that basis alone. The intended distinction is between a genuinely unseen class and an appearance shift affecting recognition. A shift can recur at another time without thereby becoming a new class; the goal is for the system to keep those possibilities separate.
But the wording does not tell us what produces the shifts, does it?

It does not. “Recurring appearance shifts” describes the kind of variation the recognizer must handle, but the goal does not name a cause, a dataset, or a particular shift pattern. Those specifics should not be assumed when stating the objective.
Nor have I picked a model or an evaluation procedure beyond those targets.

Correct. The goal specifies the recognition setting, the coexistence condition for the novelty-detection target, and the old-class retention limit. It does not select an architecture, a training method, stored substitutes for images, or a more detailed evaluation protocol.
If I describe the aim in one sentence, what should I be careful not to leave out?

Keep all four parts together: continual visual recognition; distinguishing unseen classes from recurring appearance shifts without task boundaries or stored images; novelty-detection AUROC ≥0.90 when unseen classes and those shifts coexist; and mean old-class accuracy decline of ≤5 percentage points relative to post-acquisition performance.

For that objective, I propose maintaining online class-by-appearance feature prototypes, detecting novelty through shift-marginalized class likelihoods, and rehearsing adapters on the prototypes without storing images.

That is a proposed way to connect the three parts of the problem. Class-by-appearance feature prototypes would represent known classes while allowing for differences in how they appear. Shift-marginalized class likelihoods would be used to judge novelty without equating every appearance change with a new class. Rehearsing adapters on prototypes would aim to preserve previously acquired recognition without retaining images. It is a method proposal, not yet evidence that either performance target is met.
What does “class-by-appearance” add to the idea of a class prototype?

It makes appearance variation part of what the prototypes represent. Rather than describing a class with only an undifferentiated feature summary, the proposal keeps track of class and appearance together. That matters because an appearance that differs from one familiar presentation could still belong to a known class.
Does that mean each appearance is treated as its own class?

No. The distinction is important: the prototypes are organized by class and appearance, but a variation in appearance is not automatically a new class. The proposal uses that organization to help distinguish recurring appearance shifts from genuinely novel classes.
And “online” means the prototypes are maintained as experience continues?

Yes. Maintaining them online means updating or maintaining the feature-level representation during continual recognition rather than assuming it is assembled once from a complete, fixed collection. The proposal does not specify an update rule, how often updates occur, or how many prototypes there are.
Are the prototypes themselves stored images?

No—the proposal calls them feature prototypes and explicitly says not to store images. They are intended as feature-level representations, not retained copies of the visual inputs. The exact form of those features is not specified.
I want to be precise about novelty detection. What is the role of the class likelihoods?

The proposed novelty decision is based on how well known classes can account for an observation, expressed through class likelihoods. The key qualification is that those likelihoods are shift-marginalized: appearance shifts are accounted for when assessing whether a known class is plausible. The proposal does not specify a likelihood formula or a decision threshold.
How is that different from simply flagging anything that looks unlike one prototype?

Looking unlike one prototype could reflect an appearance shift rather than an unseen class. A shift-marginalized class likelihood is meant to assess known-class plausibility while taking appearance variation into account, instead of treating a mismatch to one appearance representation as sufficient evidence of novelty.
Does “marginalized” require me to claim a particular mathematical procedure here?

No particular procedure is stated. At the conceptual level, it means the novelty assessment accounts for possible appearance shifts when evaluating a class, rather than tying the decision to just one appearance condition. The details of how those possibilities are represented or combined remain unspecified.
So the novelty signal should concern class novelty, not just a new-looking appearance?

Exactly as an aim of the proposal. Its novelty-detection component is intended to ask whether known classes remain plausible after accounting for appearance shifts. That is distinct from labeling an observation novel solely because its appearance is unfamiliar.
Where do adapters come into the proposal?

The proposal says to rehearse adapters on the feature prototypes. In broad terms, the prototypes provide something representing previously acquired knowledge for that rehearsal, and the adapters are the components being rehearsed. It does not say how the adapters are structured or how rehearsal updates them.
Why rehearse on prototypes instead of on stored examples?

Because the proposed setting does not store images. Rehearsing on prototypes is the proposed way to revisit feature-level representations of known classes without retaining the original images. Whether that suffices to meet the old-class accuracy constraint would still have to be assessed; it is not established by the proposal alone.
Does the proposal imply that the entire recognizer is retrained during rehearsal?
No. It specifically names adapters as what would be rehearsed on prototypes. It does not state that the entire recognizer is retrained, nor does it define which other components, if any, change.
How do the prototype and likelihood parts fit together conceptually?

The prototypes maintain feature-level representations organized by class and appearance. The shift-marginalized likelihoods are the proposed basis for deciding whether an observation is plausibly from a known class despite an appearance shift. Those are complementary roles: representing familiar variation and evaluating class novelty in light of it. The proposal does not pin down the exact computation connecting them.
And the rehearsal part serves a different requirement?

It is directed toward retaining recognition of previously acquired classes while operating without stored images. That aligns with the goal of limiting mean old-class accuracy decline from post-acquisition performance to ≤5 percentage points. The novelty component is directed toward the separate AUROC ≥0.90 target when unseen classes and recurring appearance shifts coexist. Both remain targets, not reported outcomes.
Would this approach need explicit task boundaries to know when to maintain the prototypes?

The proposal is framed for a setting without task boundaries, and online prototype maintenance is consistent with continuing operation rather than relying on announced task changes. It does not, however, specify the mechanism for deciding when to update a prototype or how to handle every ambiguous observation.
Could I say that it has already solved the confusion between recurring shifts and unseen classes?

No. You can say the proposed shift-marginalized likelihoods are intended to address that confusion. The node describes an approach, not a demonstrated result, so it does not establish that the novelty-detection AUROC target or the old-class retention limit has been achieved.
What should remain open when describing the proposal?

Among the unspecified details are the feature representation, the number and updating of prototypes, the calculation of shift-marginalized class likelihoods, the novelty decision rule, and the adapter rehearsal procedure. Keeping those open preserves the proposal as stated without adding implementation choices.
Can you restate the proposal without turning any of those open details into decisions?

Maintain class-by-appearance feature prototypes online; use shift-marginalized class likelihoods to detect genuinely novel classes while accounting for appearance shifts; and rehearse adapters on those prototypes without storing images. It is a proposed approach to continual visual recognition under the stated constraints, with performance against the AUROC and old-class accuracy targets still to be determined.
Which prototype score would distinguish a returning camera style from a new class when each known class spans multiple styles?

That is the unresolved scoring question. A score based on mismatch to just one prototype could mistake a known class in another camera style for a new class. The relevant comparison would have to consider the appearance prototypes associated with each known class and ask whether any known class remains plausible after accounting for style. The proposal names shift-marginalized class likelihoods, but it does not yet define the prototype score or how those likelihoods are computed.
Why isn't a close match to a prototype in the returning style enough?

A style match alone addresses appearance, not class identity. The score needs to distinguish evidence that the observation belongs to a known class in that style from evidence that it merely shares the style with known observations. Otherwise a genuinely new class photographed in a familiar style could look reassuringly familiar for the wrong reason.
So a familiar camera style should not automatically count as a familiar class?

Right. A returning camera style is an appearance condition; a new class concerns what is being recognized. The question is how prototype-based evidence can keep those two kinds of familiarity separate when every known class may have multiple appearances.
What comparison does the word “returning” suggest?

It suggests an appearance style encountered before appearing again. But its return does not, by itself, settle the class decision. The proposed score would still need to assess whether a known class accounts for the observation under that style, rather than making the style's recurrence the novelty decision.
Would scoring only against the closest prototype answer the question?

Not automatically. A closest-prototype score is one possible quantity to examine, but the question asks whether it distinguishes class familiarity from style familiarity across multiple styles per class. A close match could require interpretation in terms of both the class and the appearance represented by that prototype. No choice of a closest-prototype rule has been made here.
What does considering multiple styles per known class change?

It means a poor match to one appearance of a class need not be a poor match to the class overall. Conversely, seeing a familiar appearance style somewhere among the prototypes need not make every class observed in that style familiar. The score has to evaluate known-class plausibility across the class's appearances without collapsing class identity into style.
Is that what the shift-marginalized class likelihood was meant to address?

Conceptually, yes: it was proposed to assess class likelihood while accounting for appearance shifts. Your question presses on the missing detail—what evidence from class-by-appearance prototypes yields a class score that remains meaningful when styles recur and each known class has several of them. Calling it shift-marginalized does not, on its own, supply that calculation.
Could the score just measure whether the current style has been seen before?

That would answer a different question. It might indicate familiarity of the camera style, but novelty detection here concerns unseen classes in the presence of recurring appearance shifts. The class score must not treat a familiar style as sufficient evidence that the class is known.
Could the opposite mistake happen—calling a known class new because its style differs from one of its prototypes?

Yes, that is the other conceptual error the question highlights. When a known class spans multiple styles, a score tied too narrowly to one appearance could reject the class despite another of its appearances being relevant. The scoring question is how to use the class-by-appearance information without making either error.
Does the question imply that all known classes have exactly the same styles?

No. It says each known class spans multiple styles; it does not specify which styles each class has, whether their coverage is identical, or how many prototypes represent them. A scoring answer should not depend on those unstated details being fixed.
Would a high score for one known class be interpreted differently from a high score for a camera style alone?

Yes, at the conceptual level. A high known-class score would mean the observation is plausibly accounted for as that class while allowing for its appearances. A high style-only score would mean the appearance condition seems familiar. The scoring question is precisely how to produce and interpret the former without substituting the latter.
How would that connect to calling an observation novel?

Novelty would concern whether the known classes can adequately account for it after appearance variation is considered. But the question has not supplied a score definition, a rule for comparing known classes, or a threshold for declaring novelty. It would be premature to specify those as if they were settled.
Should the score somehow compare class evidence across styles, rather than comparing styles without regard to class?

That captures the distinction being sought. Whatever prototype score is chosen would need to preserve the association between a known class and its possible appearances. Simply pooling evidence for a camera style across classes could obscure whether any particular known class fits.
Is there a determined answer here, such as one particular similarity or likelihood formula?

Not from the stated question and proposal alone. They identify the desired behavior and the idea of shift-marginalized class likelihoods, but not a particular similarity measure, likelihood formula, aggregation across style prototypes, or decision threshold. Those remain open aspects of the score.
Then what, exactly, am I asking the score to distinguish?

You are asking for prototype-based evidence that separates two cases: an observation of a known class under a camera style that has returned, and an observation of a genuinely new class that may also share familiar appearance characteristics. Because each known class spans multiple styles, the evidence must be interpreted at the class level while accounting for those styles—not as a novelty judgment about camera style alone.

I have a hypothesis for the prototype score: the maximum classwise style-marginalized Mahalanobis likelihood will achieve novelty-detection AUROC ≥0.90 and outperform nearest-prototype distance on recurring shifts.

That gives a specific answer to the scoring question, while remaining a hypothesis rather than a measured result. For each known class, the proposed score accounts for its styles in a Mahalanobis-based likelihood; it then takes the maximum across classes. The prediction is both novelty-detection AUROC ≥0.90 and better performance than nearest-prototype distance on recurring shifts.
Why take the maximum across classes?

Conceptually, the maximum asks whether any known class can account well for the observation after that class's styles have been considered. That is different from asking whether the observation resembles a familiar camera style somewhere. The hypothesis does not specify a numerical rule for converting the resulting maximum into a novelty decision.
What does “classwise” prevent me from losing?

It keeps the style assessment attached to each candidate class. You would form a style-marginalized likelihood for a class, then compare those class-level likelihoods. Merely finding evidence for a familiar style without regard to class would not answer whether the observed class is known.
And the order matters: account for styles within each class before taking the maximum?

Yes—that is what “maximum classwise style-marginalized likelihood” conveys. The score being maximized is already a classwise likelihood that accounts for style. It is not simply the best match to one class-by-style prototype taken in isolation.
Does style-marginalized mean selecting whichever style prototype happens to be closest?

Not necessarily. Marginalizing over styles and choosing a single nearest prototype are distinct scoring ideas. The hypothesis specifies style-marginalized Mahalanobis likelihoods but does not give their exact calculation, so it would be premature to equate that marginalization with selecting one closest style.
What does the Mahalanobis part contribute to the description?

It specifies the kind of feature-space measure underlying the proposed likelihood, rather than leaving the score as an unspecified notion of similarity. The hypothesis does not state how that likelihood is parameterized or estimated. Those details cannot be filled in as though they were part of the claim.
If a known class appears under a returning camera style, what is the score intended to reflect?

It is intended to reflect whether that known class plausibly accounts for the observation after its possible styles are taken into account. The return of the camera style alone is not enough; the classwise likelihood still has to concern class membership. The hypothesis predicts that this distinction will help on recurring shifts, but it has not established that it does.
And if the camera style is familiar but the class is new?

The intended distinction is that familiarity of the style should not by itself produce strong evidence for a known class. The maximum classwise score asks whether any known class accounts for the observation, not merely whether some style has appeared before. Whether the proposed score reliably makes that distinction is part of the hypothesis.
Why compare it specifically with nearest-prototype distance?

Nearest-prototype distance is the named comparison baseline for this prediction. The hypothesis is not just that the proposed likelihood reaches novelty-detection AUROC ≥0.90; it also predicts that it outperforms nearest-prototype distance on recurring shifts. No numerical margin of improvement is specified.
Am I claiming nearest-prototype distance can never recognize a returning style correctly?
No. The claim is comparative performance on recurring shifts, not that the baseline always fails. Nor does the hypothesis say how either score performs in every individual case.
Could I describe the predicted advantage as coming from accounting for multiple styles of each class?

You can describe that as the motivation: the proposed likelihood accounts for styles within each class rather than relying solely on the nearest prototype. But the advantage itself remains predicted. The hypothesis does not contain evidence showing that this motivation produces the stated AUROC or outperformance.
Is the ≥0.90 value a threshold for each observation's likelihood?
No. It is the hypothesized novelty-detection AUROC target, not a cutoff for the likelihood score. The node does not specify a likelihood threshold for declaring an individual observation novel.
Does the outperformance claim mean an AUROC improvement on recurring shifts?

The hypothesis places the comparison in the context of recurring shifts, but it does not explicitly name a separate metric for that comparison. It does explicitly name novelty AUROC ≥0.90 as a target for the proposed score. It is safest to preserve both claims as written rather than assign an unstated numerical measure or margin to the comparison.
Does this hypothesis establish anything about old-class accuracy decline?

No. It concerns the novelty score and its predicted performance relative to nearest-prototype distance on recurring shifts. The separate goal of limiting mean old-class accuracy decline from post-acquisition performance to ≤5 percentage points remains part of the broader objective, but this hypothesis does not assert that the limit has been met.
Nor does it say that adapter rehearsal has succeeded?

Correct. Adapter rehearsal on prototypes is part of the proposed approach, but this particular hypothesis is about the maximum classwise style-marginalized Mahalanobis likelihood as a novelty score. It states no rehearsal outcome.
How should I phrase the prediction without making it sound like an experimental result?

You could say: “We hypothesize that the maximum classwise style-marginalized Mahalanobis likelihood will achieve novelty-detection AUROC ≥0.90 and outperform nearest-prototype distance on recurring shifts.” That retains the proposed score, the numerical target, the comparison, and their status as a prediction.
What remains unspecified in that sentence?

It does not define the exact Mahalanobis likelihood, the way styles are marginalized, a novelty decision threshold, or the magnitude and measure of the predicted advantage over nearest-prototype distance. Those omissions should remain open rather than being supplied as unannounced decisions.

To evaluate the novelty-score hypothesis, I want to run boundary-free DomainNet streams with recurring domains and held-out classes, then compare novelty AUROC for classwise marginal likelihood versus nearest-prototype distance.

That sets out an evaluation activity, not a result. The boundary-free streams retain the no-task-boundary condition; recurring domains bring back appearance variation; and held-out classes provide the unseen-class side of the novelty distinction. Comparing the two scores by novelty AUROC would address the predicted advantage of classwise marginal likelihood over nearest-prototype distance.
Why include recurring domains in the streams?

They make the comparison relevant to the question of whether a returning appearance condition is mistaken for a new class. A score could respond to a returning domain's changed appearance without correctly distinguishing that shift from class novelty. Including recurrence puts that distinction in view.
And what role do the held-out classes play?

They provide classes that the recognizer should treat as unseen in the novelty evaluation. With held-out classes and recurring domains both present, the comparison concerns class novelty amid appearance changes rather than novelty detection in isolation.
Does “boundary-free” mean the streams have no changes in them?

No. The streams can contain recurring domains and held-out classes without supplying task boundaries that announce changes. “Boundary-free” describes the absence of those task markers, not the absence of variation in what the recognizer encounters.
Am I specifying an order in which the domains must recur?
No particular order or frequency of recurrence is stated. The activity calls for DomainNet streams with recurring domains, but it does not define their schedule.
Have I identified which DomainNet classes to hold out?
Not in this activity. It specifies held-out classes as part of the streams, without naming the classes or giving a selection rule.
What exactly is being compared?

The comparison is novelty AUROC for the classwise marginal-likelihood score versus novelty AUROC for nearest-prototype distance on those streams. The earlier hypothesis describes the proposed score more fully as a maximum classwise style-marginalized Mahalanobis likelihood; this activity names its classwise marginal-likelihood side without adding a new scoring formula.
Why use novelty AUROC for the comparison?

It is the named novelty-detection measure in the activity and in the hypothesis being evaluated. Comparing AUROC keeps the focus on how the scores distinguish unseen classes from known-class observations across possible decision thresholds. This activity does not specify a single threshold for either score.
Does running that comparison automatically establish novelty AUROC ≥0.90?
No. The ≥0.90 value is the hypothesized target. The streams and comparison are a way to evaluate it; no AUROC values or conclusions from a run are provided here.
What if I say the classwise score outperforms nearest-prototype distance on these streams?
As a prediction, that matches the hypothesis. As a statement of an observed outcome, it would go beyond this activity, which specifies the comparison but reports no results.
Does the activity also specify a measured margin between their AUROCs?
No. It calls for comparing novelty AUROC, but gives neither score's AUROC nor a required numerical difference between them.
Is the point to see whether a familiar domain alone gets treated as evidence of a familiar class?

That is the conceptual distinction the evaluation can probe. A domain's recurrence reflects familiar appearance variation, while a held-out class concerns class novelty. The proposed classwise score is intended to account for appearance variation without treating domain familiarity alone as proof that a class is known.
Does this activity settle how the marginal likelihood is calculated?

No. It names the scores to compare, but does not provide the likelihood calculation, the handling of multiple style prototypes, or an implementation of nearest-prototype distance. Those details are not results or decisions stated by this node.
What about the no-stored-images constraint from the overall goal?

It remains a constraint on the continual-recognition setting. This activity does not introduce image storage or specify a storage procedure; its stated focus is running boundary-free DomainNet streams and comparing the two novelty scores.
Should this comparison be described as testing adapter rehearsal too?
Not on the information given. The activity compares novelty AUROC for two scores. It does not state an adapter-rehearsal comparison or report a result for retaining old-class accuracy.
So it also cannot tell me yet whether mean old-class accuracy decline is ≤5 percentage points from post-acquisition performance?

Correct. That remains a separate requirement of the broader goal. This activity specifies a novelty-AUROC comparison, not an old-class accuracy measurement or an outcome against the ≤5-percentage-point limit.
How would you state this as an action without implying it has already been done?

“Run boundary-free DomainNet streams containing recurring domains and held-out classes, and compare novelty AUROC for classwise marginal likelihood against nearest-prototype distance.” That describes the intended evaluation without asserting an AUROC value or declaring either score better.
On boundary-free DomainNet, the style-marginalized likelihood achieved 0.93 novelty AUROC, versus 0.84 for nearest-prototype distance.

The reported result is a direct novelty-AUROC comparison on boundary-free DomainNet: 0.93 for style-marginalized likelihood and 0.84 for nearest-prototype distance. The style-marginalized score is higher by 0.09 AUROC in this comparison.
Can you put the comparison into words without losing the numbers?

On boundary-free DomainNet, style-marginalized likelihood produced a novelty AUROC of 0.93, while nearest-prototype distance produced 0.84. Thus, the reported novelty-detection measure was higher for style-marginalized likelihood in this evaluation.
Is 0.09 an accuracy difference?
No. It is the difference between the reported AUROC values: 0.93 minus 0.84. These figures measure novelty detection by AUROC, not classification accuracy or the decline in old-class accuracy.
What does the result say about a particular novelty decision threshold?

It does not give one. AUROC summarizes discrimination across possible thresholds; the reported values do not specify which threshold would be used for an individual decision or how many individual observations were classified correctly at that threshold.
Does “boundary-free” mean this result assumes task transitions are announced?

No. The reported setting is boundary-free DomainNet, so the comparison is not described as relying on announced task boundaries. The result does not provide a more detailed account of how the streams were processed.
I was concerned about confusing a recurring appearance with a new class. Is that the setting for this comparison?

The DomainNet streams specified for the comparison contain recurring domains and held-out classes, bringing recurring appearance variation and unseen classes into the evaluation. The reported evidence is the two overall novelty-AUROC values; it does not provide a separate breakdown for particular returns of a domain or particular held-out classes.
Does the 0.93 tell us that every returning domain was handled correctly?
No. An overall novelty AUROC of 0.93 does not establish perfect handling of every observation or every returning domain. There is no per-domain result in the reported evidence.
Could I say that nearest-prototype distance scored 0.84 on the same reported evaluation?
Yes. The evidence presents the values as a comparison on boundary-free DomainNet: 0.93 for style-marginalized likelihood versus 0.84 for nearest-prototype distance.
Is the result a comparison of novelty detection, rather than of how well the two approaches recognize old classes?
Yes. Both reported numbers are novelty AUROC. The evidence does not report old-class accuracy or a change in that accuracy from post-acquisition performance.
Can I infer anything here about prototype-based adapter rehearsal?
No rehearsal outcome is given in this result. It reports the novelty-AUROC comparison between two scores, not an evaluation of adapter rehearsal or image-free retention performance.
Does the evidence give the exact formula for the style-marginalized likelihood?

No. It names the score and reports its AUROC, but does not specify the likelihood formula or how the styles were combined in its computation. Those details should not be inferred from the two values alone.
And it doesn't specify how nearest-prototype distance was computed?
Correct. Nearest-prototype distance is the named comparator, with a reported novelty AUROC of 0.84. The evidence does not add a distance formula or further implementation details.
How far can I generalize from the DomainNet numbers?
The stated evidence is specific to boundary-free DomainNet. It does not report results on other datasets, nor does it give a basis for assigning the same AUROC values to other settings.
Are these averages with uncertainty intervals?

The evidence provides 0.93 and 0.84 as the achieved novelty-AUROC values, but does not say whether they are averages, how many runs there were, or whether uncertainty intervals were calculated. It would add unsupported detail to describe them that way.
If I mention the size of the advantage, should I call it nine percentage points?

It is clearest to call it a difference of 0.09 in AUROC, since the reported figures are AUROC values on a zero-to-one scale. That avoids confusing the novelty-AUROC comparison with a percentage-point change in old-class accuracy.
What is the narrowest faithful statement of the observation?

On boundary-free DomainNet, style-marginalized likelihood achieved 0.93 novelty AUROC, compared with 0.84 for nearest-prototype distance. No additional performance breakdown or retention result is reported in this observation.
Let's adopt style-marginalized likelihood for novelty scoring because its DomainNet AUROC exceeded nearest-prototype distance by 0.09.

The decision is to use style-marginalized likelihood as the novelty score. The stated reason is its 0.09 higher DomainNet AUROC relative to nearest-prototype distance. That comparison supports the choice of score; it does not, by itself, decide other parts of the continual-recognition approach.
Am I adopting it for all recognition decisions, or specifically for detecting novelty?
Specifically for novelty scoring. The decision does not say to replace every class-recognition or adaptation component with the likelihood score.
What does the 0.09 refer to?

It is the difference between the two novelty-AUROC values on DomainNet, with style-marginalized likelihood higher than nearest-prototype distance. It is not a 0.09 change in old-class accuracy or a threshold applied to an individual likelihood.
Should I describe that as a relative improvement of 0.09?

It is clearer to call it an absolute difference of 0.09 in AUROC. “Relative improvement” could imply a different calculation, whereas the decision states that one DomainNet AUROC exceeded the other by 0.09.
Why is nearest-prototype distance mentioned in the decision?

It is the comparison for the stated reason. The decision favors style-marginalized likelihood for novelty scoring because its DomainNet AUROC was 0.09 higher than that comparator's. It does not claim that nearest-prototype distance fails in every situation.
Does adopting the likelihood mean a returning appearance must always be classified correctly?
No. The decision selects a novelty score on the basis of a reported comparative AUROC. It makes no guarantee about every returning appearance or every individual novelty decision.
Is this a decision to store images so the likelihood can be computed?

No. Image storage is not part of this decision. It chooses style-marginalized likelihood for novelty scoring, without adding a storage method or changing the no-stored-images constraint of the broader goal.
Have we also decided exactly how to calculate the likelihood?

This decision names the score to adopt but does not supply its formula, parameters, or an individual-observation cutoff. Choosing the scoring approach should not be restated as though those implementation details were specified here.
Does the AUROC difference tell me what cutoff to use to call a class new?
No. AUROC is a measure across possible decision thresholds. A 0.09 advantage in DomainNet AUROC gives the stated reason for selecting the score, but it does not identify an operating cutoff.
Does this choice settle the question of how well previously acquired classes are retained?
